# Derandomizing Pseudopolynomial Algorithms for Subset Sum

**Abstract**

We reexamine the classical _subset sum_ problem: given a set _X_ of _n_ positive integers and a number _t_, decide whether there exists a subset of _X_ that sums to _t_; or more generally, compute the set <u>OUT</u> of all numbers \(y\in\{0,\dots,t\}\) for which there exists a subset of _X_ that sums to _y_. Standard dynamic programming solves the problem in _O(tn_) time. In SODA’17, two papers appeared giving the current best deterministic and randomized algorithms, ignoring polylogarithmic factors: Koiliaris and Xu’s deterministic algorithm runs in \(\widetilde{O}(t\sqrt{n})\) time, while Bringmann’s randomized algorithm runs in \(\widetilde{O}(t)\) time. We present the first deterministic algorithm running in \(\widetilde{O}(t)\) time.

Our technique has a number of other applications: for example, we can also derandomize the more recent output-sensitive algorithms by Bringmann and Nakos [S’20] and Bringmann, Fischer, and Nakos [SODA’25] running in \(\widetilde{O}(|\mathrm{OUT}|^{4/3})\) and \(\widetilde{O}(|\mathrm{OUT}|\sqrt{n})\) time, and we can derandomize a previous fine-grained reduction from 0-1 knapsack to min-plus convolution by Cygan et al. [ICALP’17].

### 1 Introduction

This paper studies one of the textbook problems in algorithm design, the _subset sum_ problem: given a (multi)set _X_ of _n_ positive integers and a target number _t_, decide whether there exists a subset of _X_ that sums to _t_. The problem is weakly NP-complete. Standard algorithms achieve roughly _O_(2<sup>_n/_2</sup>) time (by the meet-in-the-middle trick [HS74]) and _O(tn_) time (by dynamic programming [Bel57]). Although it has remained open whether the exponential bound 2<sup>_n/_2</sup> could be improved in the worst case, the pseudopolynomial bound _O(tn_) has been improved: in two concurrent SODA’17 papers, Koiliaris and Xu [KX19] described a deterministic \(\widetilde{O}(t\sqrt{n})\)-time algorithm,<sup>1</sup> and Bringmann [Bri17] described a randomized (Monte Carlo) \(\widetilde{O}(t)\)-time algorithm. Another elegant randomized (Monte Carlo) \(\widetilde{O}(t)\)-time algorithm was found by Jin and Wu [JW19].

All of these pseudopolynomial algorithms can solve a stronger "all-targets" version of the problem: compute \(\mathrm{OUT}=\{y\in\{0,\dots,t\}:\text{there exists a subset of}X\text{that sums to}y\}\). They can also compute a representation of a feasible subset for each \(y\in\mathrm{OUT}\) (so that a subset may subsequently be reported in \(\widetilde{O}(1)\) time per element). For the all-targets version of the problem, the randomized \(\widetilde{O}(t)\)-time algorithms are clearly near optimal since the output size is \(\Omega(t)\) in the worst case. For the original version of the problem, Abboud, Bringmann, Hermelin, and Shabtay [ABHS22] also ruled out algorithms with time bounds of the form \(O(t^{1-\varepsilon} 2^{o(n)})\) for any constant \(\varepsilon>0\), assuming SETH (see also [CDL<sup>+</sup>16] for an earlier conditional lower bound under a different hypothesis).

In recent years, numerous other algorithms have been proposed for the subset sum problem that take into account different parameters (e.g., the output size |OUT| \[BN20, BFN25\], the largest input value max(_X_) \[PRW21, CLMZ24a, CLMZ24b\], the density \[BW21\], space usage \[LN10, Bri17, JVW21, NW21, BCKM24\], _..._). Many variants have also been explored (e.g., unbounded subset sum \[Bri17\], modular subset sum \[ABJ<sup>+</sup>19, ABB<sup>+</sup>21, CI21\], approximate subset sum \[KMPS03, CLMZ24a\], _..._), and the problem is connected to other fundamental problems such as knapsack and coin changing, forming a very active topic of current research.

## Derandomization?

The results in the two SODA’17 papers naturally raise the question of whether there exists a _deterministic_ \(\widetilde{O}(t)\)-time algorithm for subset sum, and this question has remained open for the last 8 years. Bringmann’s randomized algorithm uses a color-coding technique \[AYZ95\], and although some past algorithms based on color-coding have been successfully derandomized (e.g., for computing _k_-simple paths/cycles in graphs), the overhead for derandomizing color-coding seems too big for the application to subset sum (our desired \(\widetilde{O}(t)\) bound doesn’t leave much room to absorb the overhead). If the number of elements _k_ allowed in a sum is sublogarithmic, the cost of derandomization is tolerable, but not when _k_ is large. It is unclear how to apply standard techniques such as the method of limited independence or the method of conditional probabilities/expectations without blowing up the time bound. Jin and Wu’s alternative randomized algorithm \[JW19\] seems even tougher to derandomize--it computes counts modulo a random prime, and there is no obvious efficient way to guarantee that a correct prime is selected. Just converting these Monte Carlo randomized algorithms to Las Vegas is already open. On the other hand, Koiliaris and Xu’s deterministic approach \[KX19\] (see also \[KX18\] for an alternative) seems difficult to improve upon--they did give a variant with \(\widetilde{O}(t^{4/3})\) running time but there is no clear path towards \(O(t^{1+\varepsilon})\). By contrast, for variants such as unbounded subset sum<sup>2</sup> \[Bri17\] and modular subset sum \[ABB<sup>+</sup>21\], efficient derandomization is not as difficult and is already known.

## New algorithm.

We present the first deterministic algorithm for subset sum running in \(\widetilde{O}(t)\) time. It also solves the all-targets version of the problem.

Our algorithm may be viewed as a derandomization of a variant of Bringmann’s \[Bri17\]. Instead of partitioning the input set into multiple disjoint subsets via color-coding, we recursively partition the input set into two subsets, in such a way that the desired subset for each target is split roughly evenly into two halves in terms of their cardinalities (with about \(\sqrt{k}\) additive error if the subset has about _k_ elements). This reinterpretation of Bringman’s algorithm as a divide-and-conquer via "halvers" (or similar randomized partitioning) is not new, and has appeared in other subsequent randomized algorithms for subset sum and knapsack (e.g., see \[BN20, BDP24, BFN25\]). However, although the existence of a good halver is guaranteed by the probabilistic method (via standard Chernoff or discrepancy bound), its deterministic construction seems to require knowing the subsets for all targets, i.e., knowing all the answers in the first place! Our new approach is to speed up the halver construction by worsening its quality.<sup>3</sup> So long as the additive error is kept slightly sublinear (bounded by _k/_log_k_), the divide-and-conquer would still be efficient. To this end, we show that for any subset, there is an equivalent subset (with the same sum) that can be divided into a sublinear number of small "canonical" subsets; we then naively construct a halver with respect to these<tbc>

<sup>2</sup>In the unbounded subset sum problem, we may use an element multiple times to sum to the target. This tends to be easier, as much of the challenge in the original problem is in preventing an element from being used more than once. <sup>3</sup>The idea is very loosely inspired by work on derandomization in computational geometry concerning "\(\varepsilon\)-nets" and "\(\varepsilon\)- approximations" \[Cha01, Mat00\]. One specific inspiration is the author’s derandomization of a recursive algorithm for linear programming in low dimensions \[Cha18\], which builds a lower-quality \(\varepsilon\)-net (sufficient for this recursive algorithm) simply by dividing the input set into small subsets and applying a slow \(\varepsilon\)-net algorithm to each subset.

canonical subsets. The quality of the halver with respect to the original subsets would indeed suffer, but since there are not too many canonical subsets overall and their sizes are small, the construction is cheaper. But how to generate good canonical subsets? Our idea is to adapt Koiliaris and Xu’s deterministic algorithm for this purpose! Putting these pieces together in the right way, the whole solution turns out to be relatively simple, describable in 3 pages (see Section 2).

### Other consequences.

Our new idea on halver construction can help derandomize other algorithms, too. We mention two applications:

1. Bringmann and Nakos \[BN20\] and Bringmann, Fischer, and Nakos \[BFN25\] recently obtained randomized _output-sensitive_ algorithms for the all-targets version of the subset sum problem, running in \(\widetilde{O}(|\mathrm{OUT}|^{4/3})\) and \(\widetilde{O}(|\mathrm{OUT}|\sqrt{n})\) time respectively. (Standard dynamic programming \[Bel57\] can be made to run in \(\widetilde{O}(|\mathrm{OUT}|n)\) time.) Our technique can derandomize both algorithms with the same time bound up to polylogarithmic factors in _n_ and _t_.<tbc>

2. Cygan, Mucha, Węrzycki, and Włodarczyk \[CMWW19\] gave a randomized reduction showing that if the min-plus convolution problem for _n_ elements could be solved in \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) time, then the 0-1 knapsack problem for items with positive integer weights bounded by _t_ and positive real profits could be solved in randomized \(\widetilde{O}(t^{2-\varepsilon^\prime})\) time. Our technique provides a derandomization of this result. (Derandomizing reductions have gained more attention recently; e.g., see \[CH20, CX24, FKP24\].) In particular, this implies a deterministic \(O(t^2/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}t})})\)-time algorithm for 0-1 knapsack, by using Chan and Williams’ deterministic min-plus matrix multiplication algorithm \[CW21\] together with a known reduction from min-plus matrix multiplication to convolution \[BCD<sup>+</sup>14\].

The second application above follows immediately by our technique (see Appendix A). The first application is more interesting, however, and requires additional new ideas, as we can no longer apply Koiliaris and Xu’s approach to generate canonical subsets (see Section 3).

### Notation.

Let \[_u_\] denote {0,1_,...,u_}. For a set _S_ of integers, let \(\sigma(S)=\sum_{s\in S}s\). Define

\(\Sigma_i(X)=\{y:\exists S\subseteq X\text{with}|S|=i\text{and}\sigma(S)=y\}.\)

Let \(\Sigma_{\le k}(X):=\bigcup_{i\in[k]}\Sigma_i(X)\), and \(\Sigma(X)=\Sigma_{\le\infty}(X)\). The all-targets version of the subset sum problem is to compute \(\Sigma(X)\cap[t]\) for a given _t_.

## 2 An \(\widetilde{O}(t)\)-Time Algorithm

In this section, we present a deterministic \(\widetilde{O}(t)\)-time algorithm for all-targets subset sum.

### 2.1 Preliminaries: Review of Koiliaris and Xu’s algorithm

Many previous work on subset sum starts by considering the related problem of computing \(\Sigma_{\le k}(X)\) (or a superset) for a given _k_. Bringmann \[Bri17\] solved this version of the problem in randomized \(\widetilde{O}(ku)\) time, where _u_=max(_X_), whereas Koiliaris and Xu \[KX19\] solved it in deterministic \(\widetilde{O}(k^2u)\) time. We first review Koiliaris and Xu’s solution, as we will need it later. Their approach is a binary divide-and-conquer, using convolutions as a subroutine. We describe a simplified version below, running in \(\widetilde{O}(k^3u)\) time, which is good enough for our application; we reinterpret the divide-and-conquer in terms of dyadic intervals.

**Lemma 2.1.** _Given a set X of integers in_ \[_u_\] _and a number k, we can compute_ \(\Sigma_i(X)\) _for all_ \(i\in[k]\)_, in_ \(\widetilde{O}(k^3u)\) _deterministic time._

_Afterwards, for any given_ \(i\in[k]\) _and_ \(y\in\Sigma_i(X)\)_, we can report one subset_ \(S\subseteq X\) _with_ |_S_|=_i and_ \(\sigma(S)=y\)_, in_ \(\widetilde{O}(k)\) _time._

_Proof._ W.l.o.g., assume that _u_ is a power of 2. A _dyadic interval_ is an interval of the form \((a,a+\ell]\) where the length \(\ell\) is a power of 2 and _a_ is divisible by \(\ell\). For each dyadic interval \(I=(a,a+\ell]\subseteq(0,u]\), we want to compute \(\{\Sigma_i(X\cap I)\}_{i\in[k]}\).

Decompose _I_ into two dyadic subintervals \(I'=(a,a+\ell/2]\) and \(I''=(a+\ell/2,a+\ell]\). We can compute \(\{C_i:=\Sigma_i(X\cap I)\}_{i\in[k]}\) from \(\{A_{i^\prime}:=\Sigma_{i^\prime}(X\cap I')\}_{i^\prime\in[k]}\) and \(\{B_{i^{\prime\prime}}:=\Sigma_{i^{\prime\prime}}(X\cap I'')\}_{i^{\prime\prime}\in[k]}\) by the formula \(C_i=\bigcup_{i^\prime,i^{\prime\prime}:i^\prime+i^{\prime\prime}=i}(A_{i^\prime}+B_{i^{\prime\prime}})\). Since \(A_{i^\prime}\subseteq(ai',(a+\ell/2)i']\) and \(B_{i^{\prime\prime}}\subseteq((a+\ell/2)i'',(a+\ell)i'']\) are contained in intervals of length \(O(k\ell)\) for each \(i',i''\in[k]\), we can compute each sumset \(A_{i^\prime}+B_{i^{\prime\prime}}\) via a convolution of two Boolean vectors of length \(O(k\ell)\) in \(O(k\ell log(k\ell))\) time. For each element \(z\in A_{i^\prime}+B_{i^{\prime\prime}}\), we can also compute a _witness_ \((x,y)\in A_{i^\prime}\times B_{i^{\prime\prime}}\) with _x+y=z_, in \(O(k\ell log^{O(1)}(k\ell))\) time using the deterministic witness-finding technique by Alon and Naor \[AN96\].<sup>4</sup> The total cost over all _O(k_<sup>2</sup>) choices of \((i',i'')\) is \(O(k^3\ell log^{O(1)}\ell)\). For each element \(z\in C_i\), we can also record an \((i',i'')\) with \(i'+i''=i\) and \(z\in A_{i^\prime}+B_{i^{\prime\prime}}\).

Proceeding bottom-up over all dyadic intervals, which have total length _O(u_log_u_), we obtain a total running time of \(\widetilde{O}(k^3u)\). For the root interval _I_<sub>0</sub>=(0_,u_\], we can report a subset corresponding to a given \(i\in[k]\) and \(y\in\Sigma_i(X\cap I_0)\) in \(\widetilde{O}(k)\) time by backtracking using the witnesses to the convolutions.

_(Note._ Koiliaris and Xu’s original version of the algorithm \[KX19\] achieved \(\widetilde{O}(k^2u)\) time instead of \(\widetilde{O}(k^3u)\), essentially by observing that the _C<sub>i</sub>_’s can be computed by a single convolution of vectors of length \(O(k^2\ell)\), instead of _O(k_<sup>2</sup>) convolutions of vectors of length \(O(k\ell)\). Also, they performed the divide-and- conquer slightly differently, by sorting the elements _x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>n</sub>_ of _X_ and computing \(\{\Sigma_i(\{x_j:j\in I\})\}_{i\in[k]}\) for dyadic intervals \(I\subseteq(0,n]\). This allows some log_u_ factors to be replaced by log_n_, which isn’t important to us, although this alternative will be useful later in Section 3.)

## 2.2 Halver

The key idea behind our algorithm concerns the construction of a _halver_, which we define below:

**Definition 2.2.** _Given a set X of positive integers, and numbers k and_ \(\Delta\)_, a_ \((k,\Delta)\)-halver _of X is a partition of X into two disjoint subsets_ \(X'\) _and_ \(X''\) _with the following property:_

_For every subset_ \(S\subseteq X\) _with_ \(|S|\le k\)_, there exists a subset_ \(\hat{S}\subseteq X\) _with_ \(|\hat{S}|\le k\), \(\sigma(\hat{S})=\sigma(S)\)_, and_ \(|\hat{S}\cap X'|,|\hat{S}\cap X''|\le|\hat{S}|/2+\Delta\).

Note the slight subtlety with the existential quantifier in the above definition (since there could be multiple subsets with the same cardinality and the same sum as _S_). We recall a well-known fact from discrepancy theory:

**Lemma 2.3.** _Given a set X and a collection_ C _of subsets of X each of size at most k, we can compute a partition of X into two subsets_ \(X'\) _and_ \(X''\) _such that_ \(|S\cap X'|,|S\cap X''|\le|S|/2+O(\sqrt{|S|log|\mathcal{C}|})\) _for all_ \(S\in\mathcal{C}\)_, in O(k_|C|+|_X_|) _deterministic time._

<sup>4</sup>Alon and Naor’s witness-finding technique was originally described for matrix multiplication, but the technique is general and applies to convolution.

_Proof._ The existence of such a partition \((X',X'')\) is a basic fact in discrepancy theory \[Cha01\]. (A random partition works with high probability by a simple application of the Chernoff bound.) A deterministic construction of \((X',X'')\) can be obtained by the method of conditional expectation; see \[Cha01, Theorem 1.2\] for a good description.<sup>5</sup>

The above lemma implies the existence of a \((k,\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{k}))\)-halver: for each \(y\in[ku]\), we simply fix one subset \(S\subseteq X\) with \(|S|\le k\) and \(\sigma(S)=y\), if exists, and add it to the collection C, and then apply Lemma 2.3 to this collection. However, the construction time is too large (we would have to solve the subset sum problem in order to construct the collection C in the first place!). To improve the construction time, we worsen the additive error of our halver from \(\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{k})\) to \(\widetilde{O}(k/\sqrt{b})\) for a parameter \(b\le k\). We accomplish this by building a collection of small "canonical" subsets of sizes at most _b_, generated from Koiliaris and Xu’s algorithm, and then apply Lemma 2.3 to construct a halver for this collection:

**Lemma 2.4** (Canonical subset generation)**.** _Given a set X of integers in_ \[_u_\] _and a number b, we can generate a collection_ C _of_ \(\widetilde{O}(b^2u)\) _"canonical" subsets of X each of size at most b, in_ \(\widetilde{O}(b^3u)\) _deterministic time, satisfying the following property:_

_For every subset_ \(S\subseteq X\)_, there exists a subset_ \(\hat{S}\subseteq X\) _such that_ \(|\hat{S}|=|S|\), \(\sigma(\hat{S})=\sigma(S)\)_, and_ \(\hat{S}\) _is expressible as a union of O_((|_S|/b_+1)log_u_) _disjoint canonical subsets in_ C.

_Proof._ Run the algorithm from the proof of Lemma 2.1 with _k=b_. For each dyadic interval \(I=(a,a+\ell]\), \(i\in[b]\), and \(y\in\Sigma_i(X\cap I)\), find one subset \(S_I[i,y]\subseteq X\cap I\) with |_S<sub>I</sub>_\[_i,y_\]|=_i_ and \(\sigma(S_I[i,y])=y\), and add the subset to the collection C. The number of such subsets is \(O(b^2\ell)\) per _I_ (since there are _b_ choices of _i_ and \(O(\ell b)\) choices of \(y\in(ai,(a+\ell)i]\)), each of which can be generated in \(\widetilde{O}(b)\) time. Over all dyadic intervals _I_ (which have total length _O(u_log_u_)), the total number of subsets is \(\widetilde{O}(b^2u)\).

To prove that C satisfies the stated property, consider an arbitrary subset \(S\subseteq X\). First partition (0_,u_\] into a collection I(_S_) of disjoint dyadic intervals, each containing at most _b_ points of _S_: namely, we start by visiting the root dyadic interval, and when we visit a dyadic interval containing more than _b_ points of _S_, we recursively visit its two child intervals. The number of dyadic intervals visited per level is _O_(|_S|/b_+1). Thus, the number of dyadic intervals generated is \(|\mathcal{I}(S)|\le O((|S|/b+1)logu)\). For each interval \(I\in\mathcal{I}(S)\), let \(i_I=|S\cap I|\in[b]\) and \(y_I=\sigma(S\cap I)\in\Sigma_i(X\cap I)\). Define \(\hat{S}\) to be the union of _S<sub>I</sub>_\[_i<sub>I</sub>,y<sub>I</sub>_\] over all \(I\in\mathcal{I}(S)\); these sets \(S_I[i_I,y_I]\subseteq X\cap I\) are obviously disjoint because the intervals in I(_S_) are disjoint; and \(|S_I[i_I,y_I]|=|S\cap I|\) and \(\sigma(S_I[i_I,y_I])=\sigma(S\cap I)\). Therefore, \(|\hat{S}|=|S|\) and \(\sigma(\hat{S})=\sigma(S)\).

**Lemma 2.5** (Fast halver construction)**.** _Given a set X of integers in_ \[_u_\] _and_ \(b\le k\)_, we can compute a_ \((k,\widetilde{O}(k/\sqrt{b}))\)_-halver of X in_ \(\widetilde{O}(b^3u)\) _deterministic time._

_Proof._ Apply Lemma 2.4 to construct a collection C of \(\widetilde{O}(b^2u)\) canonical subsets in \(\widetilde{O}(b^3u)\) time. Then apply Lemma 2.3 to this collection C, with _k_ replaced by _b_, to compute a partition \((X',X'')\) in \(\widetilde{O}(b^3u)\) time.

To prove that \((X',X'')\) satisfies the \((k,\widetilde{O}(k/\sqrt{b}))\)-halver property, consider an arbitrary subset \(S\subseteq X\) with \(|S|\le k\). Let \(\hat{S}\subseteq X\) be such that \(|\hat{S}|=|S|\le k\), \(\sigma(\hat{S})=\sigma(S)\), and \(\hat{S}\) is expressible as a union of _O_((_k/b_)log_u_) disjoint canonical subsets \(S_j\in\mathcal{C}\). We have \(|S_j\cap X'|,|S_j\cap X''|\le|S_j|/2+\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{b})\) for each such subset _S<sub>j</sub>_. Summing over _S<sub>j</sub>_ gives \(|\hat{S}\cap X'|,|\hat{S}\cap X''|\le|\hat{S}|/2+\widetilde{O}(k/b\cdot\sqrt{b})\).

<sup>5</sup>The time bound stated there was _O_(|_X_||C|), but because all our subsets have sizes at most _k_, the running time of the algorithm is actually _O(k_|C|+|_X_|).

### 2.3 Putting everything together

Finally, we use halvers to obtain a deterministic divide-and-conquer algorithm for subset sum (which may be viewed as a variant of Bringmann’s randomized algorithm \[Bri17\]):

**Lemma 2.6.** _Given a set X of integers in_ \[_u_\] _and a number k, we can compute a set_ \(\mathrm{OUT}\subseteq[ku]\) _such that_ \(\Sigma_{\le k}(X)\subseteq\mathrm{OUT}\subseteq\Sigma(X)\)_, in_ \(\widetilde{O}(ku)\) _deterministic time._

_Proof._ The algorithm proceeds as follows:

1. Compute a (_k,k/_log_k_)-halver \((X',X'')\) of _X_ in \(\widetilde{O}(u)\) time, by applying Lemma 2.5 with _b_=log_<sup>c</sup>(ku_) for a sufficiently large constant _c_ (assuming _k\>b_).<tbc>

2. Recursively solve the problem for the input set \(X'\) and number _k/_2+_k/_log_k_; let \(\mathrm{OUT}'\subseteq[ku]\) be the output set. Recursively solve the problem for the input set \(X''\) and number _k/_2+_k/_log_k_; let \(\mathrm{OUT}''\subseteq[ku]\) be the output set.<tbc>

3. Return the clipped sumset \(\mathrm{OUT}=(\mathrm{OUT}'+\mathrm{OUT}'')\cap[ku]\), which can be computed by a convolution two Boolean vectors of length _O(ku_) in \(\widetilde{O}(ku)\) time.

The running time satisfies the recurrence:

\(T(k,u)=2T(k/2+k/\mathrm{log}k,u)+\widetilde{O}(ku).\)

For the base case \(k\le b\) (which implies \(k\le\mathrm{log}^{O(1)}u\)), we can use Lemma 2.1 to compute \(\Sigma_{\le k}(X)\) in \(\widetilde{O}(u)\) time and thus get \(T(k,u)=\widetilde{O}(u)\). The recurrence solves to \(T(k,u)=\widetilde{O}(ku)\).

To prove correctness, consider a subset \(S\subseteq X\) with \(|S|\le k\) and \(\sigma(S)=y\). By definition of halver, there exists a subset \(\hat{S}\subseteq X\) with \(|\hat{S}|\le k\), \(\sigma(\hat{S})=y\), and \(|\hat{S}\cap X'|,|\hat{S}\cap X''|\le k/2+k/\mathrm{log}k\). Then \(\sigma(\hat{S}\cap X')\in\mathrm{OUT}'\) and \(\sigma(\hat{S}\cap X'')\in\mathrm{OUT}''\) by induction, and so \(y=\sigma(\hat{S}\cap X')+\sigma(\hat{S}\cap X'')\in\mathrm{OUT}\).

**Theorem 2.7.** _Given a set X of n integers in_ \[_t_\]_, we can compute_ \(\Sigma(X)\cap[t]\) _in_ \(\widetilde{O}(t)\) _deterministic time._

_Proof._ For each \(i\in[\lceil\mathrm{log}t\rceil]\), let \(X_i=X\cap(t/2^i,t/2^{i-1}]\). Compute \(\Sigma(X_i)\cap[t]\) by applying Lemma 2.6 with _u=t/_2<sup>_i_-1</sup> and _k_=2_<sup>i</sup>_ in \(\widetilde{O}(2^i\cdot t/2^{i-1})=\widetilde{O}(t)\) time (this is because \(\Sigma(X_i)\cap[t]=\Sigma_{\le 2^i}(X_i)\cap[t]\) when \(X_i\subseteq(t/2^i,\infty)\)). We return the clipped sumset \(((\Sigma(X_0)\cap[t])+(\Sigma(X_1)\cap[t])+\cdots)\cap[t]\), which can be computed by _O_(log_t_) convolutions of Boolean vectors of length _O(t_) in \(\widetilde{O}(t)\) time.

## 3 Output-Sensitive Algorithms

In this section, we describe another application of our technique: the derandomization of a recent output- sensitive algorithm for all-targets subset sum by Bringmann, Fischer, and Nakos \[BFN25\], which runs in \(\widetilde{O}(|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|\sqrt{n})\) time. An earlier output-sensitive algorithm by Bringmann and Nakos \[BN20\], which runs in \(\widetilde{O}(|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|^{4/3})\) time, can also be derandomized in a similar way, as we will briefly mention at the end.

## 3.1 Preliminaries

We begin with a known subroutine on output-sensitive computation of sumsets. This subproblem was first solved by Cole and Hariharan \[CH02\] with randomization, which was later derandomized/improved in a series of subsequent papers \[CL15, BFN21, BFN22, JX24\]:

**Lemma 3.1.** _Given two sets A and B of integers in_ \[_t_\]_, we can compute the sunset A+B in_ \(\widetilde{O}(|A+B|)\) _deterministic time._

Output-sensitive computation of clipped sumsets is more expensive. Bringmann and Nakos \[BN20\] described a simple approach yielding the following (using the subroutine in Lemma 3.1):

**Lemma 3.2.** _Given two sets A and B of integers in_ \[_t_\]_, we can compute the clipped sunset_ \(C=(A+B)\cap[t]\) _in_ \(\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{|A||B||C|})\le\widetilde{O}((|A|+|C|)\sqrt{|B|})\) _deterministic time._

The next lemma below, observed by Bringmann, Fischer, and Nakos \[BFN25, Lemma 3.1\] (but stated in a different form), derandomizes the small _k_ case using Bringmann’s color-coding approach \[Bri17\]. For completeness, we include a quick proof sketch:

**Lemma 3.3.** _Given a set X of n integers in_ \[_t_\]_, a set A of integers in_ \[_t_\]_, and a number k, we can compute a set_ \(\mathrm{OUT}\) _such that_ \((A+\Sigma_{\le k}(X))\cap[t]\subseteq\mathrm{OUT}\subseteq(A+\Sigma(X))\cap[t]\)_, in_ \(\widetilde{O}(k^{O(1)}|(A+\Sigma(X))\cap[t]|\sqrt{n})\) _deterministic time._

_Afterwards, for any given_ \(y\in\mathrm{OUT}\)_, we can report one number_ \(a\in A\) _and one subset_ \(S\subseteq X\) _with_ \(a+\sigma(S)=y\)_, in_ \(\widetilde{O}(|S|)\) _time._

_Proof._ There exists a family H of _O(k_<sup>_O_(1)</sup>log_n_) "perfect" hash functions from _X_ to {1_,...,k_<sup>2</sup>} satisfying the following property: for every subset \(S\subseteq X\) with \(|S|\le k\), there exists \(h\in\mathcal{H}\) such that \(\{h(x):x\in S\}\) are all distinct. The family can be constructed in _O(k_<sup>_O_(1)</sup>log<sup>_O_(1)</sup>_n_) time. E.g., see \[AYZ95, Section 4\].

Fix \(h\in\mathcal{H}\). For each \(j\in\{1,\dots,k^2\}\), let \(X_{h,j}=\{x\in X:h(x)=j\}\). Compute the clipped sumset

\(\mathrm{OUT}_h=(A+(X_{h,1}\cup\{0\})+\cdots+(X_{h,k^2}\cup\{0\}))\cap[t]\)

by applying Lemma 3.2 _O(k_<sup>2</sup>) times in \(\widetilde{O}(k^{O(1)}|(A+\Sigma(X))\cap[t]|\sqrt{n})\) time. Then \(\mathrm{OUT}=\bigcup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\mathrm{OUT}_h\) fulfills the output requirement. For any given \(y\in\mathrm{OUT}\), we can report a corresponding number \(a\in A\) and subset \(S\subseteq X\) again using the deterministic witness-finding technique by Alon and Naor \[AN96\].

## 3.2 Halver

As before, the key idea is the construction of a halver. We now need a "weighted" variant that halves the sum of a subset rather than its cardinality:

**Definition 3.4.** _Given a set X of positive integers, and numbers t and_ \(\Delta\)_, a_ weighted \((t,\Delta)\)-halver _of X is a partition of X into two disjoint subsets_ \(X'\) _and_ \(X''\) _with the following property:_

_For every subset_ \(S\subseteq X\) _with_ \(\sigma(S)\le t\)_, there exists a subset_ \(\hat{S}\subseteq X\) _with_ \(\sigma(\hat{S})=\sigma(S)\)_, and_ \(\sigma(\hat{S}\cap X'),\sigma(\hat{S}\cap X'')\le\sigma(\hat{S})/2+\Delta\).

As before, we will generate a collection of small canonical subsets, to which we will then apply Lemma 2.3 to construct a halver. Unfortunately, Koiliaris and Xu’s algorithm is no longer applicable, since it is not output-sensitive. Instead, we will use the algorithm from Lemma 3.3 for small _k_ for this purpose.<tbc>

However, it is not clear how canonical subsets can be obtained from this algorithm, since it does not work via divide-and-conquer or dyadic intervals. Our new idea is to invoke the algorithm for Lemma 3.3 multiple times on different inputs associated with different dyadic intervals. Bounding the total cost of these multiple invocations may at first appear problematic, but luckily the following simple observation comes to the rescue:

**Observation 3.5.** _Let X be a sorted list of numbers. Suppose X is partitioned into contiguous sublists X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>m</sub>. Then_ \(|\Sigma_{\le k}(X_1)\cap[t]|+\cdots+|\Sigma_{\le k}(X_m)\cap[t]|\le O(k)|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|\).

_Proof._ For a fixed _i_, \(\Sigma_i(X_1),\dots,\Sigma_i(X_m)\) are disjoint, since every element in \(\Sigma_i(X_j)\) is smaller than every element in \(\Sigma_i(X_{j+1})\) for every _j_. Thus, \(|\Sigma_i(X_1)\cap[t]|+\cdots+|\Sigma_i(X_m)\cap[t]|\le|\Sigma_i(X)\cap[t]|\). The observation then follows by summing over all \(i\in[k]\).

**Lemma 3.6** (Canonical subset generation)**.** _Given a constant_ \(\delta\in(0,1]\)_, a set X of n integers in_ \([u/(1+\delta),u]\)_, and numbers t and b, we can generate a collection_ C _of_ \(\widetilde{O}(b|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|)\) _"canonical" subsets of X each of size at most_ \((1+\delta)b\)_, in_ \(\widetilde{O}(b^{O(1)}|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|\sqrt{n})\) _deterministic time, satisfying the following property:_

_For every subset_ \(S\subseteq X\) _with_ \(\sigma(S)\le t\)_, there exists a subset_ \(\hat{S}\subseteq X\) _such that_ \(\sigma(\hat{S})=\sigma(S)\) _and_ \(\hat{S}\) _is expressible as a union of O_((|_S|/b_+1)log_n_) _disjoint canonical subsets in_ C.

_Proof._ W.l.o.g., assume that _n_ is a power of 2. Sort the elements _x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>n</sub>_ of _X_. For each dyadic interval \(I=(a,a+\ell]\subseteq(0,n]\), run the algorithm in Lemma 3.3 with \(A=\emptyset\), _k=b_, and _t_ replaced by min{_t,bu_}, on the input set \(X_I:=\{x_j:j\in I\}\), to get output set \(\mathrm{OUT}_I\). For each dyadic interval _I_ and each \(y\in\mathrm{OUT}_I\subseteq\Sigma(X_I)\cap[\mathrm{min}\{t,bu\}]\), find one subset \(S_I[y]\subseteq X_I\) with \(\sigma(S_I[y])=y\), and add the subset to the collection C. Note that \(|S_I[y]|\le bu/(u/(1+\delta))=(1+\delta)b\). By Observation 3.5, the sum of \(|\Sigma(X_I)\cap[\mathrm{min}\{t,bu\}]|=|\Sigma_{\le(1+\delta)b}(X_I)\cap[\mathrm{min}\{t,bu\}]|\) over all dyadic intervals _I_ of a fixed length is at most \(O(b|\Sigma(X)\cap[\mathrm{min}\{t,bu\}]|)\); thus, the sum over all dyadic intervals _I_ of all lengths is \(O(b|\Sigma(X)\cap[\mathrm{min}\{t,bu\}]|\mathrm{log}n)\). So, the total number of subsets in C is bounded by \(O(b|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|\mathrm{log}n)\), and the computation time is \(\widetilde{O}(b^{O(1)}|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|\sqrt{n})\).

To prove that C satisfies the stated property, consider an arbitrary subset \(S\subseteq X\). First partition (0_,n_\] into a collection I(_S_) of disjoint dyadic intervals, each containing at most _b_ indices of \(\{j:x_j\in S\}\): namely, we start by visiting the root dyadic interval, and when we visit a dyadic interval containing more than _b_ indices of \(\{j:x_j\in S\}\), we recursively visit its two child intervals. The number of dyadic intervals visited per level is _O_(|_S|/b_+1). Thus, the number of dyadic intervals generated is \(|\mathcal{I}(S)|\le O((|S|/b+1)\mathrm{log}n)\). For each interval \(I\in\mathcal{I}(S)\), let \(y_I=\sigma(S\cap X_I)\in\Sigma_{\le b}(X_I)\cap[\mathrm{min}\{t,bu\}]\subseteq\mathrm{OUT}_I\). Define \(\hat{S}\) to be the union of _S<sub>I</sub>_\[_y<sub>I</sub>_\] over all \(I\in\mathcal{I}(S)\); these sets \(S_I[y_I]\subseteq X_I\) are obviously disjoint because the intervals in I(_S_) are disjoint; and \(\sigma(S_I[y_I])=\sigma(S\cap X_I)\). Therefore, \(\sigma(\hat{S})=\sigma(S)\).

**Lemma 3.7** (Fast halver construction)**.** _Given a set X of n integers in_ \[_u_\] _and numbers t and b, we can compute a weighted_ \((t,\widetilde{O}(t/\sqrt{b}+bu))\)_-halver of X in_ \(\widetilde{O}(b^{O(1)}|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|\sqrt{n})\) _deterministic time._

_Proof._ Let \(\delta=1/\sqrt{b}\). For each \(\ell\in[\lceil\mathrm{log}_{1+\delta} u\rceil]\), let \(X^{(\ell)}=X\cap[(1+\delta)^\ell,(1+\delta)^{\ell+1})\). Apply Lemma 3.6 to the input set \(X^{(\ell)}\) (with _u_ replaced by \((1+\delta)^{\ell+1}\)) to construct a collection \(\mathcal{C}^{(\ell)}\) of \(\widetilde{O}(b|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|)\) canonical subsets in \(\widetilde{O}(b^{O(1)}|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|\sqrt{n})\) time. Let \(\mathcal{C}=\bigcup_\ell\mathcal{C}^{(\ell)}\). Then apply Lemma 2.3 to this collection C, with \(k=(1+\delta)b\), to compute a partition \((X',X'')\) in \(\widetilde{O}(b^{O(1)}|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|)\) time.

To prove that \((X',X'')\) satisfies the weighted \((t,\widetilde{O}(t/\sqrt{b}+bu))\)-halver property, consider an arbitrary subset \(S\subseteq X\) with \(\sigma(S)\le t\). Let \(\hat{S}^{(\ell)}\subseteq X^{(\ell)}\) be such that \(\sigma(\hat{S}^{(\ell)})=\sigma(S\cap X^{(\ell)})\) and \(\hat{S}^{(\ell)}\) is expressible<tbc>

as a union of \(O((|S\cap X^{(\ell)}|/b+1)\mathrm{log}n)\) disjoint canonical subsets \(S_j^{(\ell)}\in\mathcal{C}^{(\ell)}\). We have \(|S_j^{(\ell)}\cap X'|,|S_j^{(\ell)}\cap X''|\le|S_j^{(\ell)}|/2+\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{b})\) for each such subset _Sj_. Summing over \(S_j^{(\ell)}\) gives \(\mathrm{max}\{|\hat{S}^{(\ell)}\cap X'|,|\hat{S}^{(\ell)}\cap X''|\}\le|\hat{S}^{(\ell)}|/2+\widetilde{O}((|S\cap X^{(\ell)}|/b+1)\cdot\sqrt{b})\)
\(=|\hat{S}^{(\ell)}|/2+\widetilde{O}(|S\cap X^{(\ell)}|/\sqrt{b}+\sqrt{b}).\) Let \(\hat{S}=\bigcup_\ell\hat{S}^{(\ell)}\). Then \(\sigma(\hat{S})=\sigma(S)\). Now, \(\frac{1}{1+\delta}\sigma(\hat{S}\cap X')\le\sum_\ell(1+\delta)^\ell|\hat{S}^{(\ell)}\cap X'|\), and \(\frac{1}{1+\delta}\sigma(\hat{S}\cap X'')\le\sum_\ell(1+\delta)^\ell|\hat{S}^{(\ell)}\cap X''|\). Thus, \(\mathrm{max}\{\sigma(\hat{S}\cap X'),\sigma(\hat{S}\cap X'')\}\le\sum_\ell(1+\delta)^\ell\left(|\hat{S}^{(\ell)}|/2+\widetilde{O}(|S\cap X^{(\ell)}|/\sqrt{b}+\sqrt{b})\right)+O(\delta t)\)
\(\le\sigma(\hat{S})/2+\widetilde{O}\left(\sigma(S)/\sqrt{b}+\sum_\ell(1+\delta)^\ell\sqrt{b}\right)+O(\delta t)\)
\(=\sigma(\hat{S})/2+\widetilde{O}(t/\sqrt{b}+\sqrt{b}u/\delta+\delta t)=\sigma(\hat{S})/2+\widetilde{O}(t/\sqrt{b}+bu).\) ## 3.3 Putting everything together We are now ready to derandomize Bringmann, Fischer, and Nakos’ algorithm \[BFN25\]. The algorithm is a multi-way divide-and-conquer, so we first extend halvers to split into _r_ parts: **Definition 3.8.** _Given a set X of positive integers, and numbers t and_ \(\Delta\)_, a_ weighted _r_-way \((t,\Delta)\)-splitter _of X is a partition of X into r disjoint subsets X_1_,...,Xr with the following property:_ _For every subset_ \(S\subseteq X\) _with_ \(\sigma(S)\le t\)_, there exists a subset_ \(\hat{S}\subseteq X\) _with_ \(\sigma(\hat{S})=\sigma(S)\)_, and_ \(\sigma(\hat{S}\cap X_j)\le\sigma(\hat{S})/r+\Delta\) _for each_ \(j\in\{1,\dots,r\}\). **Corollary 3.9** (Fast _r_-way splitter construction)**.** _Given a set X of n integers in_ \[_u_\] _and numbers t,b,r, we can compute a weighted r-way_ \((t,\widetilde{O}((t/\sqrt{b}+bu)\mathrm{log}r))\)_-splitter of X in_ \(\widetilde{O}(rb^{O(1)}|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|\sqrt{n})\) _deterministic time._ _Proof._ Just apply Lemma 3.7 recursively for log_r_ levels. **Theorem 3.10.** _Given a set X of n integers in_ \[_t_\]_, we can compute_ \(\Sigma(X)\cap[t]\) _in_ \(\widetilde{O}(|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|\sqrt{n})\) _deterministic time._ _Proof._ Let \(u_S=\lceil t/(r^6\mathrm{log}^ct)\rceil\) for a sufficiently large constant _c_. Let \(X_S=X\cap[u_S]\) and \(X_L=X\cap(u_S,t]\). The following is a reinterpretation of Bringmann, Fischer, and Nakos’ algorithm \[BFN25\]: 1. Compute a weighted _r_-way (_t,t/r_2)-splitter (_X_1_,...,Xr_) of _XS_ in \(\widetilde{O}(r^{O(1)}|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|\sqrt{n})\) deterministic time, by applying Corollary 3.9 with \(b=\widetilde{O}(r^4)\) and _u_ replaced by _uS_ (the parameters are chosen so that \((t/\sqrt{b}+bu_S)\mathrm{log}r\checkmark t/r^2\)). 2. Recursively compute \(A_j=\Sigma(X_j)\cap[t/r+t/r^2]\) for each \(j\in\{1,\dots,r\}\). 3. Compute the sumset \(A=A_1+\cdots+A_r\) by applying Lemma 3.1 _O(r_) times in \(\widetilde{O}(r|A|)\) deterministic time.

4. Return \((A+\Sigma(X_L))\cap[t]\), which can be computed by applying Lemma 3.3 with _k=r_<sup>6</sup>log_<sup>c</sup>t_ in \(\widetilde{O}(r^{O(1)}|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|\sqrt{n})\) deterministic time (this is because \(\Sigma(X_L)\cap[t]=\Sigma_{\le r^6\mathrm{log}^c t}(X_L)\cap[t]\) when \(X_L\subseteq(t/(r^6\mathrm{log}^ct),\infty)\)).<tbc>

<tbc>Bringmann, Fischer, and Nakos \[BFN25\] proved that

\(|(\Sigma(X_1)\cap[t/r(1+1/r)])+\cdots+(\Sigma(X_r)\cap[t/r(1+1/r)])|\le|\Sigma(X_1\cup\cdots\cup X_r)\cap[t]|^{1+1/(r-1)}\)

by using a "submultiplicativity" property for sumsets due to Gyarmati, Matolcsi, and Ruzsa \[GMR10\]. Thus, \(|A|=|A_1+\cdots+A_r|\le|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|^{1+1/(r-1)}\). Bringmann, Fischer, and Nakos further noted that \(|A_1|+\cdots+|A_r|\le|A_1+\cdots+A_r|+r-1\).

Thus, the running time for \(\mu=|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|\) satisfies the recurrence

\(T(n,t,\mu)\le\mathrm{max}_{n_1,\dots,n_r,\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r:n_1+\cdots+n_r\le n,\mu_1+\cdots+\mu_r\le\mu^{1+1/(r-1)}+r-1}\big(T(n_1,t/r+t/r^2,\mu_1)+\cdots+T(n_r,t/r+t/r^2,\mu_r)+\widetilde{O}(r^{O(1)}\cdot(\mu^{1+1/(r-1)}+\mu\sqrt{n}))\big).\)

By choosing _r_=log<sup>2</sup>_t_+1, we have \(\mu^{1/(r-1)}\le 2^{\mathrm{log}\mu/\mathrm{log}^2t}\le 2^{1/\mathrm{log}t}=1+O(1/\mathrm{log}t)\), and the recurrence solves to \(T(n,t,\mu)=\widetilde{O}(\mu\sqrt{n})\).

To close, we mention that another output-sensitive subset sum algorithm by Bringmann and Nakos \[BN20\] can be similarly derandomized. They described a (more complicated) alternative to Lemma 3.2 on output- sensitive construction of clipped sumsets, running in \(\widetilde{O}(|C|^{4/3})\) time (their construction is deterministic, if a deterministic version of Lemma 3.1 is used). By replacing Lemma 3.2, keeping the rest of the algorithm the same, and straightforwardly modifying the above analysis, we immediately obtain:

**Theorem 3.11.** _Given a set X of n integers in_ \[_t_\]_, we can compute_ \(\Sigma(X)\cap[t]\) _in_ \(\widetilde{O}(|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|^{4/3})\) _deterministic time._

## 4 Remarks

In the \(\widetilde{O}(t)\)-time algorithm in Section 2, we have not tried to optimize (and thus have not written out) the number of log_t_ factors. It is larger than the previous randomized algorithms (Bringmann’s algorithm \[Bri17\] had 4 log factors, and Jin and Wu’s algorithm \[JW19\] had 2), but is not gigantic (probably below 20).

In the output-sensitive algorithms in Section 3, we reiterate that the hidden extra factors are polylogarithmic in _n_ and _t_. The previous randomized algorithms by Bringmann, Fischer, and Nakos \[BFN25\] actually got factors that are polylogarithmic in the output size \(|\Sigma(X)\cap[t]|\) rather than in _t_; this seems harder to do from the derandomization perspective (but would not make a big difference except in some extreme cases).

Like previous work, our algorithms easily adapt to the setting when _X_ is a multiset--a subset of _X_ cannot use an element more times than its original multiplicity. (Note that _n_ could be larger than _t_ here, and to avoid an _O(n_) term in the running time, we may need to assume that _X_ is represented as a list of distinct elements with given multiplicities.)

In the \(\widetilde{O}(t)\)-time algorithm in Section 2, we generate canonical subsets by adapting Koiliaris and Xu’s algorithm \[KX19\], but in Section 3, we have realized that Koiliaris and Xu’s algorithm is not essential to our technique (though it is convenient, since it already incorporates dyadic intervals). This realization may potentially help in future applications.

We hope that our technique may find many further applications in derandomizing other algorithms in this area, since a number of previous algorithms used randomized partitioning similar to halvers--to name just two examples, Chen, Lian, Mao, and Zhang’s \(\widetilde{O}(n+\sqrt{ut})\)-time subset sum algorithm [CLMZ24b] (where _u_=max(_X_)) and Bringmann, Dürr, and Polak’s knapsack algorithm [BDP24]. We leave the question of their derandomization to future work (these algorithms have other components that may pose additional challenges to derandomize).

## A Reducing 0-1 Knapsack to Min-Plus Convolution

In the _all-capacities_ version of the _0-1 knapsack problem_, we are given _n_ items where the _j_-th item has positive integer weight _w<sub>j</sub>_ and positive real profit _p<sub>j</sub>_, and we are given a number _t_. For each \(i\in[t]\), we want to compute \(f[i]=max\left\{\sum_{j\in J}p_j:\sum_{j\in J}w_j=i,J\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}\right\}\).

0-1 knapsack may be viewed as a two-dimensional variant of subset sum. More precisely, we map each item to a point (_w<sub>j</sub>,p<sub>j</sub>_) in two dimensions. For a set of two-dimensional points \(A\subseteq[t]\times\mathbb{R}^+\), define the<tbc>

<tbc>operator \(\mathsf{p}\text{-}\mathsf{MAX}(A)=\left\{(w,p^*)\in A:p^*=max_{(w,p)\in A}p\right\}\). The problem is then equivalent to the following: given a set of _n_ two-dimensional points \(X\subset[t]\times\mathbb{R}^+\), compute \(\mathsf{p}\text{-}\mathsf{MAX}(\Sigma(X)\cap([t]\times\mathbb{R}^+))\), where \(\Sigma(\cdot)\) is defined exactly as before (additions are now performed in two dimensions). We may assume that \(n\le t\) after an initial _O(n_)-time preprocessing (replacing _X_ with \(\mathsf{p}\text{-}\mathsf{MAX}(X\cap([t]\times\mathbb{R}^+))\)).

Cygan, Mucha, Węrzycki, and Włodarczyk \[CMWW19\] and Künnemann, Paturi, and Schneider \[KPS17\] gave deterministic reductions from min-plus convolution to all-targets 0-1 knapsack. In the reverse direction, Cygan et al. \[CMWW19\] gave a _randomized_ reduction from all-targets 0-1 knapsack to min-plus convolution, by modifying Bringmann’s randomized algorithm for subset sum \[Bri17\]. We can obtain a deterministic reduction from all-targets 0-1 knapsack to min-plus convolution by modifying the algorithm in Section 2.

The modification is mostly straightforward. We mention some of the main changes:

• Expressions such as \(X\cap I\) should be reinterpreted as \(X\cap(I\times\mathbb{R}^+)\).<tbc>

• Most occurrences of \(\Sigma_i(X)\) should be changed to \(\mathsf{p}\text{-}\mathsf{MAX}(\Sigma_i(X))\).<tbc>

• Each sumset _A+B_ should be changed to \(\mathsf{p}\text{-}\mathsf{MAX}(A+B)\). Given \(A,B\subseteq[t]\times\mathbb{R}^+\), the computation of \(\mathsf{p}\text{-}\mathsf{MAX}(A+B)\) is equivalent to max-plus convolution over two real vectors of length _O(t_), which is equivalent to min-plus convolution by negation.<tbc>

• In Definition 2.2 on halvers, the property is now:<tbc>

<tbc>For every subset \(S\subseteq X\) with \(|S|\le k\) and \(\sigma(S)\in\mathsf{p}\text{-}\mathsf{MAX}(\Sigma_{\le k}(X))\), there exists a subset \(\hat{S}\subseteq X\) with \(|\hat{S}|\le k\), \(\sigma(\hat{S})=\sigma(S)\), and \(|\hat{S}\cap X'|,|\hat{S}\cap X''|\le|\hat{S}|/2+\Delta\).<tbc>

• In Lemma 2.4 on canonical subset generation, the property is now:<tbc>

<tbc>For every subset \(S\subseteq X\) with \(\sigma(S)\in\mathsf{p}\text{-}\mathsf{MAX}(\Sigma_{|S|}(X))\), there exists a subset \(\hat{S}\subseteq X\) such that \(|\hat{S}|=|S|\), \(\sigma(\hat{S})=\sigma(S)\), and \(\hat{S}\) is expressible as a union of _O_((|_S|/b_+1)log_u_) disjoint canonical subsets in C.<tbc>

<tbc>Note that if \(\sigma(S)\in\mathsf{p}\text{-}\mathsf{MAX}(\Sigma_{|S|}(X))\), then for any interval _I_, we must also have \(\sigma(S\cap(I\times\mathbb{R}^+))\in\mathsf{p}\text{-}\mathsf{MAX}_{|S\cap(I\times\mathbb{R}^+)|}(X\cap(I\times\mathbb{R}^+))\).<tbc>

• In Lemma 2.6, we are now computing a set \(\mathsf{OUT}\subseteq[ku]\times\mathbb{R}^+\) such that \(\mathsf{p}\text{-}\mathsf{MAX}(\Sigma_{\le k}(X))\subseteq\{(w,p'):p'\ge p,(w,p)\in\mathsf{OUT}\}\) and \(\mathsf{OUT}\subseteq\Sigma(X)\).

The rest of the changes are easy to work out.

**Theorem A.1.** _If min-plus convolution for two real vectors of length n could be computed in T(n_) _deterministic time, then the all-capacities version of the 0-1 knapsack problem could be solved in_ \(\widetilde{O}(T(t))\) _deterministic time._
